property_summary: Only the contract's Owner can successfully call withdraw (non-Owner calls revert).
Only calls to withdraw made by the contract Owner succeed (non-Owner callers revert).
If withdraw is called by someone who is not the contract's Owner, the call must revert (so non-owners cannot succeed in withdrawing).
Calling withdraw from any address other than C.Owner must always revert (i.e., only Owner can successfully call withdraw).
After sending some ETH to C from this contract and then calling withdraw, the call must transfer all ETH out of C so that address(c).balance == 0.
Calling withdraw should never revert when msg.sender equals the contract's Owner (i.e., the caller is Owner).
If withdraw is called by the current Owner, the call must succeed (not revert).

For any caller and any contract balance, calling withdraw by Owner transfers the entire contract balance to Owner (so address(c).balance becomes 0); the mutant sending to msg.sender can send funds to a different address and thus can leave the contract with non-zero balance or send to wrong recipient.

For any caller who is the Owner and any contract balance, calling withdraw always results in the contract balance becoming zero (reference): the mutant that transfers to msg.sender can leave the contract non-zero when the caller is not Owner or when Owner != msg.sender in the mutant scenario, so there exists an input (different caller) that makes address(c).balance != 0.

For any caller who is the Owner and any initial contract balance, calling withdraw causes the contract's balance to become zero (reference always sets address(c).balance == 0 after Owner withdraw); the mutant that pays msg.sender instead of Owner can cause address(c).balance != 0 for some inputs (when msg.sender != Owner), so the mutant is broken.

If withdraw is called by the Owner, the contract balance becomes zero afterward (Owner receives all funds); the mutant that sends to msg.sender can leave the contract non-zero when the caller is the Owner only if msg.sender != Owner, which cannot happen — so the reference always zeroes the balance after an Owner withdraw, while the mutant can fail to do so for some inputs.

For any caller who is the contract Owner and any initial contract balance, after calling withdraw the contract balance becomes zero (the Owner receives the full balance); the mutant that pays msg.sender instead of Owner can leave the contract balance non-zero for some inputs where msg.sender != Owner (i.e. when the caller is not the Owner), so the property distinguishes them.

For any caller and any amount, when Owner calls withdraw the contract's balance becomes zero (transfer either succeeds or reverts); the mutant using unchecked call can leave contract balance nonzero when the recipient (Owner) rejects or runs out of gas, breaking that guarantee for some inputs.

For any caller acting as Owner and any sent value, the reference contract always ends withdraw with address(c).balance == 0 (transfer either succeeds or reverts); the mutant using an unchecked call can leave funds in the contract when the recipient's fallback reverts, so for some inputs withdraw returns but contract balance remains > 0.

For any owner address and any starting contract balance, when Owner calls withdraw the reference C always results in the contract balance becoming zero (transfer either succeeds or the call reverts), whereas the mutant that uses an unchecked low-level call can return successfully while leaving a nonzero contract balance if the Owner's fallback reverts — so there exist inputs (an adversarial Owner that reverts on receive) that make the mutant leave funds in the contract.

Invariant: calling withdraw transfers the contract balance to the stored Owner (so address(c).balance becomes 0 and c.Owner() remains the same Owner) for all callers; the mutant that assigns Owner = msg.sender inside withdraw can cause the contract to transfer funds to a non-owner caller, violating that the contract balance becomes 0 while Owner remains unchanged.

For any caller who is the recorded Owner and any nonzero contract balance, calling withdraw sends the entire balance to the stored Owner without changing the Owner storage; the mutant that assigns Owner = msg.sender inside withdraw can change Owner to the caller and thus breaks the property for some caller values.

For every caller who is the recorded Owner and any balance, calling withdraw preserves that Owner (Owner remains equal to the caller) and empties the contract balance; the mutant that assigns Owner = msg.sender inside withdraw can make Owner change unexpectedly for some caller, so the property detects that by observing Owner after withdraw.

For any caller who is NOT the recorded Owner and for any nonzero contract balance, calling withdraw must revert (because only Owner can call); the mutant that sets Owner = msg.sender before transfer does not change the require but could be exploited via a reentrant attacker that becomes Owner during a nested call sequence and thus allows a non-owner to succeed — so the property: any non-owner caller's withdraw call always reverts on the correct contract, but the mutant can make it succeed for some non-owner via reentrancy/interaction.

For any (fuzzed) attacker address A and any nonzero deposit value v, if A calls multiplicate with adr = A while sending v such that msg.value < address(this).balance (so the multiplicate’s if-condition is false), then multiplicate must not transfer funds and address(c).balance remains unchanged; the mutant cannot affect multiplicate (it only changed withdraw), so to expose the mutant we instead exploit withdraw: if the current Owner performs withdraw after a deposit made by some other account, Owner remains the same and receives the funds — the mutant that assigns Owner = msg.sender before transferring can be exploited by a reentrant attacker that during an external call becomes Owner and causes the transfer to go to the attacker; therefore we deploy a reentrant Attacker that in its receive() calls back into c.withdraw(), and fuzz the attacker address and deposit amount so the correct contract always empties balance to the original Owner and preserves Owner, while the mutant allows the attacker to become Owner during the nested call and steal funds (test fails on mutant).
Only the Owner can cause an external call from c.Command that transfers msg.value (i.e., non-Owner callers cannot make c forward wei via Command).

property_summary: Only the contract Owner can invoke Command without it reverting (i.e., non-Owner callers' Command calls always revert).
If a non-owner calls Command paying X wei, the call must revert (only the owner may successfully execute Command with attached value).
If amount > 0 then calling c.Command with value amount from this (non-owner) contract must revert.
If amount > 0 then the call reverts for this caller

For every caller and calldata, calling Command(...) on the reference contract never reverts (the require restricts to Owner so only Owner can call and Owner's call succeeds); removing the require allows non-Owner callers to invoke Command which can cause the low-level call to a malicious callee to fail and thus make Command revert/fail for some inputs — so the reference always returns success for Command when invoked by Owner, while the mutant can be invoked by non-Owner and may fail.

For all callers and calldata, when Command(...) is invoked by the contract Owner it always returns successfully (does not revert) and leaves c's balance unchanged except for forwarded value; removing the require allows a malicious non-Owner caller to invoke Command and trigger a failing external call, causing Command to revert (or behave differently) for some fuzzed inputs.

For any caller and calldata, when the contract owner calls Command(...) the call itself always returns (does not revert) and the contract's balance after the call equals its balance before plus forwarded msg.value; the mutant (which allows non-owners to call) can be driven by a malicious non-owner callee to cause the external call to fail and thus violate the property for some fuzzed inputs.

For every caller address and value, when the Owner calls Command(addr, data) it always completes successfully (does not revert) — removing the require allows non-Owner callers to invoke Command and a malicious callee can make that call fail, so the mutant can exhibit a failing Command for some fuzzed caller/value that the reference never does.

For every address target and calldata payload and any msg.value, only the contract Owner can successfully invoke Command(target, payload) (i.e., when called by Owner the call returns/does not revert and the contract's balance increases exactly by msg.value); the mutant removing the require allows non-Owner callers to invoke Command, so a malicious non-Owner callee can make the external low-level call fail and thus produce a different observable outcome for some fuzzed inputs.

Invariant: Calling Command(...) as the Owner never changes the contract's Owner state (Owner remains the original deployer) — the delegatecall mutant can break this by executing code that overwrites Owner.

For any caller and any value v sent to Command, when the caller is Owner the reference contract forwards the same msg.value to the callee (so the callee can receive Ether), whereas the mutant that always forwards value 0 breaks this by not forwarding the funds for some inputs (when msg.value>0 and callee's fallback/receive behavior depends on funds).

For any caller and any wei value sent, when Owner calls Command(target,data) the contract's balance after the call equals the prior balance plus any wei forwarded to the callee by the reference implementation (i.e. Command does not double-forward msg.value); the mutant that transfers msg.value to the target before the call can reduce the contract balance by an extra msg.value for some inputs (failing the equality).

For any caller/amount where Owner calls Command(target,data) sending value v, the reference contract's balance after the call equals its balance before the call minus any v actually forwarded by the low-level call (i.e. Command does not additionally transfer msg.value away before the call); the mutant that does payable(adr).transfer(msg.value) can further reduce the contract balance by v for some inputs (violating that balance-preservation relation).

When the Owner calls Command(target, data) sending some ETH, the reference contract never causes the contract balance to decrease by more than the ETH actually forwarded by the low-level call (i.e., it does not transfer msg.value away before calling the target); the mutant that does payable(adr).transfer(msg.value) before the call can further drain msg.value and thus make address(c).balance smaller than allowed.

For any Owner-invoked Command(target,data) with some ETH, the reference contract never ends up with a smaller balance than if the target's fallback reverted (i.e., forwarding via low-level call only removes at most the value actually accepted by the callee), whereas the mutant that does payable(adr).transfer(msg.value) before the call can unconditionally reduce the contract's balance by msg.value and thus make address(c).balance smaller for some inputs.

When Owner calls Command(target, data) sending value v, the reference never decreases its balance by more than the amount actually accepted by the target's fallback/receive (i.e., it does not unconditionally transfer msg.value away before the low-level call); the mutant that does payable(adr).transfer(msg.value) before the call can unconditionally reduce the contract balance by msg.value and thus violate this balance-preservation rule for some inputs.
